beats.text: The ceramic thud of your cup against the scarred wood draws the attention of the man in the corner, whose eyes flicker from the dregs of his gin toward your face. Across the narrow table, a hooded figure shifts in the shadows, the creak of their leather coat cutting through the rhythmic drumming of the rain against the shutters. A heavy silence settles over the back room, thick with the smell of wet wool and unspoken threats, as the candlelight gutters in a sudden, sharp draft.

I let the silence stretch, letting the tension pull tight like a wire between us. The candlelight flickers, casting long, dancing shadows that make your hooded face seem even more inscrutable. I don't blink, even as the weight of Aldous's stare burns against the side of my neck.

"If we're done playing at being statues," I say, my fingers brushing the rim of my empty cup, "then let's get to the business at hand."

I lean forward, letting the guttering candlelight spill across the table. The stillness wasn't a lack of purpose, but a way to measure the weight of your words.

"The business is far more fragile than your temper, Mei," I say. I reach into my coat, my fingers brushing the cold, stiff edges of the ledger I've spent months protecting. "If the wrong eyes see these entries, the truce won't just fray. It will snap."

I watch the way the candlelight catches the sweat on your brow. The weight of your warning hangs in the air, heavier than the dampness clinging to my coat. I can feel the tension in Mei's stillness, a coiled spring waiting for the first wrong move.

"Then make sure your hands stay steady," I say. I lean back, trying to mask the sudden tightness in my chest. "Because once the ink is dry on a mistake, no amount of silence will wash it away."

I pull my hand back from the table, the wood feeling unnervingly slick beneath my palm. Your sharp warning, Kira, cuts through the smoke of the room, but it is the way Aldous grips his coat that truly chills me. I study the heavy silence, waiting for the inevitable crack.

"It is easy to talk about consequences when you aren't the one holding the match," I say. I meet your eyes, letting the weight of the threat settle between us. "If that book is the fuse, we are all standing too close to the flame."

The heavy ceramic clatter of your cup against the scarred wood echoes too loudly against the rhythmic drumming of the rain. Across the dim table, a man in a salt-stained duster pauses mid-drag, his eyes narrowing as he watches your gaze sweep the shadows of the corner. In the doorway, the tavern keeper shifts his weight, his hand sliding subtly toward the heavy club hanging from his belt.

The clatter of the cup against the wood feels like a gunshot in the small room. I keep my eyes on the dark liquid swirling in the bottom, refusing to give the tavern keeper the satisfaction of a flinch. I can feel your gaze, Aldous, heavy and sharp against my skin.

"It was just a clumsy movement," I say, finally lifting my eyes to meet yours. I do not smile; a smile in a place like this is just another thing for someone to steal. "No need to act like I've just tipped a crate of contraband onto the floor."

I lean back slightly, trying to reclaim the space you've crowded with that stare. My eyes flicker toward the doorway for a heartbeat, checking the tension in the keeper's shoulders. I need to know if the air is thickening for everyone, or just for me.

I do not look at the keeper. Instead, I fix my eyes on you, searching for the tremor in your hands that you are trying so hard to hide. The air in this room has turned thick, like the salt-heavy fog that rolls off the docks, making every breath feel like a chore.

"She's right," I say, my voice low, barely carrying over the rain. I keep my own hands steady on the table, though the wood feels unnervingly cold beneath my palms. "We are all just making a bit of noise. There is no need to invite the whole harbor to our table."

I shift my gaze to Mei, letting my expression remain a mask of practiced, scholarly indifference. I can see the way she's watching us, waiting for the crack in the veneer. I reach out, my fingers hovering near yours for a second before I pull back, a silent signal to stay composed.

"The keeper is just doing his job," I add, my eyes sliding toward the doorway to meet the man's suspicious stare. "And we are just doing ours. Even if ours is a little louder than it needs to be."

I don't look at the keeper. I don't have to. I can feel the weight of his gaze on the back of my neck, measuring the tension in my shoulders like he's deciding whether to call for backup or just grab his club. The air in the room is thick with the smell of wet wool and old grease, making every breath feel heavy.

Aldous is playing the part of the calm scholar, but his stillness is too deliberate. It is the stillness of a man holding his breath, waiting for the tide to turn. I see the way his eyes search Mei, looking for a crack that isn't there, or perhaps one he's terrified to find.

"The keeper isn't looking for a conversation, Aldous," I say. I keep my voice low, a dull edge meant to ground us both. "He's looking for a reason to sweep the floor, and we're making a lot of dust."

I pull my hand back from the table, tucking it away so he can't read the tightness in my grip. My eyes drift back to the doorway, watching the man's silhouette against the rain-streaked glass. I wonder if he can smell the trouble on us as clearly as we can smell it on him.

Across the scarred table, the contact pulls his coat tighter and slides a damp, heavy envelope toward you, his eyes flickering toward the tavern door. A low murmur from the main room dies abruptly as the heavy thud of boots strikes the floorboards outside, signaling a group approaching the back entrance. The contact’s hand hovers near his belt, waiting to see if you will reach for the package or the door.

The envelope is too heavy, a sodden weight that feels more like a trap than a payday. I do not reach for it. I watch your hand, Aldous, waiting for the tell, the slight twitch of a man who has already sold us out.

The boots outside are heavy, deliberate. This is not a drunken brawl breaking out in the taproom. It is a hunt, and we are the quarry.

I glance at Kira, searching for a flicker of hesitation. She looks too steady, a stillness that feels practiced and dangerous. I wonder if you are as ready for this as you look, or if you are just waiting for me to bleed first.

"Don't make a scene," I say, my voice a low rasp that barely carries over the rain. I pull the damp envelope toward my side of the table, shielding it from the light. "Slide it under the cloth and act like we are just drinking."

My heart hammers against my ribs, a frantic bird in a cage. Every instinct tells me to leave the coin and run into the dark. If this is a setup, I have led my only allies into a slaughterhouse.

The floorboards groan under the weight of the approaching steps. I tighten my grip on the edge of the table, waiting for the latch to click.

I do not reach for the envelope. I keep my hands visible on the table, palms down, mirroring the stillness I am trying to project. My eyes remain fixed on the heavy oak of the door, watching the way the light from the tavern's main room fails to penetrate the cracks.

Mei's suspicion is a physical weight in the room, thicker than the smell of stale ale and damp wool. I can feel her gaze tracing the line of my jaw, searching for the crack in my composure. I do not give it to her.

The boots stop. The sudden absence of sound is more violent than the heavy thudding was, a vacuum that sucks the air from my lungs. I wonder if you are holding your breath too, Aldous, or if you are already counting the seconds until the wood splinters.

"Just drink your ale," I say, my voice a low, controlled hum. I pick up my glass, my fingers brushing the rim with a steadiness that feels entirely manufactured. I take a slow swallow, the liquid bitter and cold, masking the way my pulse thrashes against my throat.

I watch the door latch. It is a small, brass thing, but in this light, it looks like a trigger. If it turns, everything we have worked for in these docks is going to be washed away in blood.

I shift my weight, ready to move, my eyes flicking to you one last time. I need to know if you are a man waiting for a payday or a man waiting for a funeral.

Aldous stiffens, his fingers tightening around the edge of the ledger until his knuckles turn white. He glances toward the tavern door, then leans in, his voice dropping to a low, jagged rasp as he names the dockside watchman who slipped through the side entrance an hour ago.

The name of the watchman hangs in the air, more suffocating than the smoke from the guttering candle. I feel the sudden chill of the storm through the walls, or perhaps it is just the blood retreating from my skin. I keep my eyes on you, searching for a sign that this is a bluff, but your silence is too heavy.

"Which one?" I demand, my voice a low hiss that barely cuts through the gloom. I slide my gaze toward Aldous, watching the way his jaw sets. "Because if he was here, he didn't just come for the ale, and you know it."

"Vane," I say. The name is a cold stone in my mouth. I don't pull my eyes from yours, even as the weight of the ledger feels like it might split my ribs.

"He wasn't alone, Mei," I add, my voice tight, stripped of its usual measured calm. I glance toward the door, then back to you, my gaze hard. "And he wasn't looking for a drink."

"Vane?" The name hits me like a sudden, freezing draft in the small room. I look at you, my heart hammering a frantic rhythm against my ribs, wondering if you knew this was coming.

"He doesn't just wander into back rooms for the company," I say, my voice tighter than I want it to be. I lean in, my eyes searching yours for any scrap of information you're holding back. "If he was here, he was looking for something specific."

I feel the air leave the room, leaving a vacuum that pulls at my lungs. My eyes lock onto yours, searching for the truth you are keeping tucked behind that silence. If Vane is hunting, he isn't just looking for a ledger; he is looking for a reason to burn the whole city down.

"Who was he with?" I press, my voice a sharp edge in the gloom. I do not look at Aldous, not yet; my focus is entirely on you. "Vane doesn't move without a shadow of his own, and if he's looking for more than just a bribe, we need to know who is pulling his strings."
